newsitem.title: USA: Dollar thrives as French vote shakes European union.
newsitem.headline: Dollar thrives as French vote shakes European union.

text.p: The dollar rose on Tuesday as investors flocked to safe havens amid worries about the implication of France's parliamentary election for Europe's proposed monetary union.
A strong left-wing showing in France's first round of elections on Sunday sparked concern that strict European economic and monetary union (EMU) entry rules could be bent to fit political wishes.
Looser fiscal criteria for entry into EMU would hurt the German mark and thus aid the dollar, dealers said.
The dollar rose to 1.7055 marks in late trading from 1.6930 marks late Friday and to 116.67 Japanese yen from 115.65 yen. Both U.S. and British currency markets were closed on Monday for holidays.
Fuelling the EMU controversy was an announcement on Monday by France's unpopular conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe that he will resign.

One of his potential successors, French National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, sent the dollar shooting to session highs on Tuesday by saying he favours looser fiscal criteria and a larger pool of entrants in the first wave of EMU, set for 1999.
Seguin's remarks, to be published on Wednesday in the weekly magazine L'Express, were reported by wire services at midday in New York.

"Even if there is an ultimate centre-right victory, you're still looking at a weaker, laxer EMU. It will be difficult to pass any fiscal austerity measures with a large protest vote," said Andrew Hodge, a financial strategist at Bank Brussels Lambert in New York.

France's opposition socialist party, which looks set to wrest power from the ruling right-wing coalition in the second round of elections on June 1, supports EMU but places heavy emphasis on growth and jobs. It also wants Italy and Spain to join EMU in the first wave of membership in 1999.
Also bolstering the U.S. currency was data showing a surge in U.S. consumer optimism in May.
On Tuesday, the Conference Board said its index of consumer confidence surged to 127.1 -- its highest level in 28 years.
The consumer sentiment number followed a revised 118.5 in April and far exceeded forecasts of 118.1 for the May index.

"Consumer confidence at a 28-year high seemed to revive speculation of U.S. interest rate hikes. So you've got that and the French elections giving some boost to the dollar," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd in Chicago.
Higher U.S. interest rates make yields on dollar-based investments more attractive.
But the greenback's rise was temporarily slowed by simultaneous data showing a 2.4 percent decline in April existing home sales, traders said.
U.S. home sales fell to a 4.06 million unit annual rate in April from a revised 4.16 million unit pace in March. Forecasts averaged 4.09 million units, annualized.

The dollar also gained against the Swiss franc, despite its traditional status as a safe haven in times of EMU uncertainty, after senior officials at Switzerland's central bank said they were unhappy with the franc's recent strength.

Swiss National Bank President Hans Meyer said on Tuesday he was not content with the recent strengthening of the franc. This was echoed by SNB vice chairman Jean-Pierre Roth who also said the central bank was not ruling out lower money market interest rates.
The dollar rose to 1.4205 Swiss francs from 1.4033, while the British pound inched lower to $1.6311 from $1.6347.
The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3828 from C$1.3747 even though the Bank of Canada bought Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars at about C$1.3830 per dollar, traders said.
